tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section compares against std::collections::BTreeSet/BTreeMap (single-threaded) and against mutex-protected std trees (12 threads), using public Criterion code: benches/single_threaded.rs with single_threaded/set.rs and map.rs, and benches/concurrent.rs with concurrent/set.rs and map.rs (MutexStdBTreeSet/MutexStdBTreeMap). It states rustc 1.97.0-nightly (ad3a598ca 2026-05-03), the Apple M2 Pro, commit 7e3ac23 (verified) and the exact cargo bench commands. The flags are Cargo's default bench profile, because Cargo.toml has no [profile] override and the repo has no .cargo/config. That meets A under the hashify/simdutf8 precedent.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Concurrent indexset (cap 256) is ~3.2x faster than a mutex-protected std::collections::BTreeMap at 50/50, 64 B, 12 threads (0.722 ms vs 2.314 ms), and ~3.5x faster than a mutex-protected BTreeSet for the set (0.728 ms vs 2.545 ms) (derived from page data). Single-threaded full traversal is ~2.5x faster for the 8 B set (37.3 us vs 92.5 us, cap 1024) and 1.5-1.8x for the other set/map traversals (derived from page data). Inserts are 1.08-1.17x faster at cap 256 for the u64 set and the 16 B/64 B map entries, but std wins 64 B set inserts. Map update-existing is 1.17-1.53x faster (derived from page data). std BTreeMap/BTreeSet wins single-threaded get, contains and remove (remove ~1.9-2.6x faster in std).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.97.0-nightly (ad3a598ca 2026-05-03); cargo bench with Criterion 0.5.1; Cargo's default bench profile (opt-level=3), with no [profile] override in Cargo.toml and no .cargo/config
corrections.workload: Single-threaded insert/contains/remove/get/update/get_index/full-traversal/128-entry range traversal over 100,000 existing entries (8 B or 64 B set values; 16 B or 64 B map entries). Concurrent runs do 10,000 operations over 12 worker threads (90/10 and 50/50 read/write). Criterion median estimates at commit 7e3ac23, measured 2026-08-26.
corrections.caveats: Single-vendor benchmark (the author's own Criterion suite on one machine); no independent reproduction. The concurrent baseline is a mutex-wrapped std BTreeMap/BTreeSet, a weak incumbent because std has no concurrent ordered map. std still wins single-threaded get/contains/remove. The license is declared only in Cargo.toml ('Apache-2.0 OR MIT'); the repo has no LICENSE files and GitHub reports no license.

notes: The record swapped the set's 0.728 ms into the map comparison; the map's figure is 0.722 ms. Its insert range '1.08-1.5x' overstated the inserts (1.08-1.17x); 1.5x only appears for map update-existing. The master branch's last commit is 2026-08-27; the 2026-09-09 pushed_at comes from an unreviewed 'rescue/worktree-20260909' branch.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B. The numbers come from the peer-reviewed VLDB 2024 paper (PVLDB 17(11) 3442-3455), which benchmarks against RocksDB (commit 54d6286) and Leanstore, and the code is now public at microsoft/bf-tree (MIT), so the no-code cap no longer applies. It is not A: the paper names no CPU model (only a CloudLab 'sm110p' node, 32 HT at 2.4 GHz) and no rustc version, and the repo pins only an unpinned 'stable' toolchain.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 1073 stars (microsoft/bf-tree); ~313k crates.io downloads (bf-tree crate); the docs repo XiangpengHao/bf-tree-docs has 93 stars
corrections.baseline: RocksDB (commit 54d6286); the authors' own conventional B-Tree and Bδ-Tree in Rust; Leanstore (commit 677126c); TwoTree
corrections.hardware: CloudLab 'sm110p' node: 32 hyper-threads at 2.4 GHz, 128 GB RAM, 1 TB NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD (>600k IOPS), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15, ext4 (CPU model not named)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper: Rust, version not stated; io_uring kernel-polling direct IO. The current microsoft/bf-tree benchmark/Cargo.toml release profile uses opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=16, panic=abort, and rust-toolchain.toml sets channel=stable (unpinned).
corrections.workload: YCSB-like: 200M initial records of 32 bytes (16 B key, 16 B value), Zipf 0.9. Default mix is 50% reads / 50% writes with a 2 GB memory cache, larger-than-memory on NVMe. Scan, write and point-lookup workloads are compared against RocksDB, B-Trees and LSM-Trees; best of 5 runs.
corrections.caveats: The code is now public at https://github.com/microsoft/bf-tree (MIT, bf-tree crate; repo created 2025-12-19). The record's repo_url is the docs/paper-only repo (no license, last commit 2024-09-25), which still says the code is 'internal to Microsoft'. The '6x faster than a B-Tree' figure is against the authors' own in-house conventional B-Tree (Bf-Tree minus mini-pages), not a shipped library; only RocksDB and Leanstore are external baselines. The numbers are from the 2024 prototype, and no CPU model or rustc version is stated. The released benchmark/ crate (optional rocksdb/sled/redb/lmdb features) has not been shown to reproduce them. The design targets modern SSDs and small records; per the author's README, large records perform like B-Trees/LSM-Trees.

notes: The repo_url should be repointed to https://github.com/microsoft/bf-tree, and the language is now plain Rust (code released). Neither field is correctable here. The docs repo is in known_list.txt, but microsoft/bf-tree is not, so this is not a known-project duplicate. The claimed_speedup wording matches the README and the paper abstract verbatim, but the paper's default records are 32 B rather than ~100 B.

tier_reason: This is an arXiv preprint (2605.23815v1, 22 May 2026; no venue or DOI found via crossref), so it is not peer-reviewed. It has first-party numbers against stock RocksDB v8.10.0 and the ported DobLIX/TridentKV on stated hardware (2x Xeon E5-2690 v4). But no code is released and no compiler or flags are given, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against stock RocksDB v8.10.0: up to 1.77x read-only and 1.44x balanced throughput (Fig. 6), up to 2.8x read throughput at the smallest value sizes (Fig. 8), and up to 1.3x write-only throughput over RocksDB's SkipList memtable (up to ~1.5x as value size shrinks). The abstract's 'up to 1.5x write, 2.1x read vs state-of-the-art systems' is against the learned-index LSMs DobLIX and TridentKV (2.1x is vs DobLIX at the smallest values), not against RocksDB.
corrections.baseline: RocksDB v8.10.0 (plus the learned-index LSMs DobLIX and TridentKV, ported to RocksDB 8.10.0)
corrections.hardware: 2x Intel Xeon E5-2690 v4 (14 cores each, 2.60 GHz), 126 GB RAM, 500 GB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
corrections.workload: Six real-world/synthetic datasets (~55 GB each, 500M operations, 16 client threads, compression off). Write-only, balanced 1:1 and read-only mixes, YCSB A-F, and varied/mixed value sizes (UDB, ZippyDB, UP2X). MountDB uses an ALEX+ Memtable with skeletonized model reuse and a block-aware PGM (Fence) on-disk index.
corrections.caveats: Preprint only (arXiv 2605.23815, McGill; not peer-reviewed as of 2026-09-26); no code released (a GitHub search for 'MountDB' finds only an unrelated repo). The headline abstract numbers are against competing learned-index systems; the gains over stock RocksDB are up to 1.77x (default value size) or 2.8x (smallest values) for reads and ~1.3x for writes. No compiler or flags are stated.

notes: The arXiv abstract matches the record's quote exactly. The body resolves the ambiguity the record flagged: the 2.1x read and 1.5x write headline is against DobLIX/TridentKV, and the RocksDB-specific gains are listed in the corrected claimed_speedup. Keep it as a paper-only reference entry.
